items.title: 13.3 Process of Finding Derivative f'(x) by Definition

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints no text under this heading; it goes straight to 13.3.1. This short introduction is ours.
In 13.2 we met the derivative as the limit of a difference quotient:
\[f'(x) = \lim_{\delta x \to 0}\dfrac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}\]
Section 13.3 turns this definition into a working method that you can use on any function you are given.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What this section covers:
1. 13.3.1 Notation of Derivative: the different symbols for the same derivative (\(f'(x)\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), \(y'\), \(Df(x)\)), and the second form of the definition, which gives the derivative at one point \(x = a\).
2. 13.3.2 Finding \(f'(x)\) by Definition of Derivative: a fixed four-step process (Step I to Step IV), used in Examples 3, 4 and 5 for \(c\), \(x^{2}\), \(\sqrt{x}\) and \(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
Before you start, keep two facts from Units 12 and 13.2 ready:
1. \(\delta x\) is one symbol: a small change in \(x\). It is not \(\delta\) times \(x\).
2. In a limit we may cancel \(\delta x\) because \(\delta x \ne 0\) while it approaches \(0\). Putting \(\delta x = 0\) straight away gives \(\frac{0}{0}\), which tells us nothing.
